at.step: A node-per-entry table pays a pointer and an allocation per entry, and almost every probe misses the cache.

items.item: Swiss Tables exist to avoid two real costs of a node-per-entry chained table at once: the pointer-and-allocation overhead per entry, and the near-certain cache miss on every probe once a chain is followed off the main array.

at.step: A node-per-entry table pays a pointer and an allocation per entry, and almost every probe misses the cache.

items.item: The whole design turns on one idea: a single wide SIMD instruction can test a whole group's control bytes against a query's fingerprint at once, so most wrong candidates are rejected without ever touching the real key.

at.step: A group holds 16 slots. How many of them does one SIMD compare instruction actually test?

items.item: H1 and H2 do two different jobs from the same single hash value: H1 (the larger share) still does the ordinary job a hash always did — picking which group to probe; H2 (a small, fixed-width slice) becomes a cheap per-slot fingerprint, stored separately from the key.

at.step: H1 picks the element's index. H2 is stored as that slot's one-byte fingerprint.

items.item: The SIMD compare instruction itself doesn't skip empty or non-matching slots — it tests the whole group's control bytes unconditionally, in the same single operation; the control byte's value (sentinel or fingerprint) is what lets only the real candidates matter afterward.

at.step: One instruction checks a whole group's control bytes against the query's H2 byte at once.

items.item: A 7-bit fingerprint has exactly 128 possible values, so two unrelated keys land on the same one by pure chance about 1 time in 128 — this topic measures that rate directly in examples.py rather than asserting it from the bit count alone.

at.step: A 7-bit fingerprint has only a 1-in-128 chance of a false match that still needs a real key comparison.

items.item: Go's own group width (8 slots) is a real, verified difference from Abseil's original 16-wide SSE groups, not an inconsistency to smooth over — both share the same control-byte-plus-SIMD-compare mechanism, at two different widths, confirmed from each project's own current source.

Three independent, real adopters (Abseil/C++ since 2017, Rust's standard library since 1.36, Go's built-in map since Go 1.24) converged on the same control-byte-plus-SIMD-compare mechanism — each verified at research time against that project's own current documentation, not assumed from memory of an older version.

at.step: Three real, current languages and runtimes converged on this exact design, verified at research time.

items.item: Testing a whole group's control bytes in parallel is what let both Abseil and Go raise their maximum load factor compared to their prior designs, since a deep probe chain now costs about the same as a shallow one.

at.step: One instruction checks a whole group's control bytes against the query's H2 byte at once.
